Simple Linear Regression: In Class Exercise

Jiyeong Pyo

2025-10-08

Welcome to an in class exercise on simple linear regression!

library(tidyverse)

Let’s clean up our environment.

rm(list = ls())

Yale Program on Climate Communication

Now you should read in the climate belief data (climate.csv) from the Yale Program on Climate Communication: https://climatecommunication.yale.edu/visualizations-data/ycom-us/.

You will work with the variables: GW = global warming. geotype the unit of observation (e.g., county, state, etc..) geoid ID for each county geoname Name of each county gwvoteimp Estimated percentage who say a candidate’s views on GW are important to their vote priority Estimated percentage who say global warming should be a high priority for the next president and Congress

In the dataframe, we will filter only counties.

climate.df<-read_csv("~/EDE_Fall2025/Justina/ENV710/climate-1.csv")%>%
  filter(geotype=="county")
Rows: 5421 Columns: 5
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (2): geotype, geoname
dbl (3): geoid, gwvoteimp, priority

climate.df

American Community Survey data from the US Census. Read in the acs.csv file with the following variables.

Population Density (Per Sq. Mile)
Average Family Income (In 2022 Inflation Adjusted Dollars)
Average Commute to Work (In Min)

census.df<-read_csv("~/EDE_Fall2025/Justina/ENV710/acs-1.csv")
Rows: 3222 Columns: 8
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (3): state, Area Name, Qualifying Name
dbl (5): geoid, Total Population, Population Density (Per Sq. Mile), Average Family ...

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
census.df

Join the datasets together. You will notice that both dataframes have the variable geoid. We will use geoid to join the two dataframes.


join.df<-census.df%>%
  inner_join(climate.df, by=join_by(geoid==geoid))%>%
  mutate(log.pop.dens=log(`Population Density (Per Sq. Mile)`)) #making new variable of log population density.

Broad research question

What is the relationship between population density and the percentage of the population who say global warming should be a high priority for the next president and Congress (response variable) in the US?

ggplot(data=join.df, aes(x=`Population Density (Per Sq. Mile)`, y=priority))+
  geom_point()+
  labs(title = "High Priority of Global Warming ~ Population Density",
       subtitle = "",
       caption = "Data sources: American Community Survey (US Census), \n Yale Climate Communication")+
  xlab("Population density (people/square mile)")+
  ylab("High Priority to address global warming")


ggplot(data=join.df, aes(x=`log.pop.dens`, y=priority))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(method="lm")+
  labs(title = "High Priority of Global Warming ~ Log Population Density",
       subtitle = "",
       caption = "Data sources: American Community Survey (US Census), \n Yale Climate Communication")+
  xlab("log population density log(people/square mile)")+
  ylab("High Priority to address global warming")
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

NA
NA

Q1: Discuss the two scatterplots above. The raw data is positively skewed so it violates the assumption 1 while the log data is well- scattered and shows linear relation between population density and priority global warning.

In the chunk below, run a linear model that is appropriate based on scatterplots above. Name the model model.1. Be sure that your X and Y are correctly placed in the lm() function.

model.1<-lm(priority~log.pop.dens, data=join.df)
summary(model.1)

Call:
lm(formula = priority ~ log.pop.dens, data = join.df)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-16.508  -4.814  -1.048   3.898  28.974 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  40.06876    0.28275  141.71   <2e-16 ***
log.pop.dens  1.61780    0.06757   23.94   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Residual standard error: 6.851 on 3152 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1539,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1536 
F-statistic: 573.2 on 1 and 3152 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

Q2: Interpret the estimate on log.pop.dens and its statistical significance. Be clear about the null hypothesis. 1% change of population density is associated with an increase in predicted prioritization of climate change by 0.016. (When we do log, we have to times 0.01 to beta->case 1) The null hypothesis is that logged population density and the priority regarding high priority of global warming has no correlation(The beta is 0). According to the P value(P <0.0001), we can reject the null hypothesis so there is correlation between variables.

Q3: Interpret the R-squared value. The r square shows it only explains 15% of the prioritization of climate change.

Run the chunk below, use the plot() function on the model object to get the Residuals vs Fitted Plot

Q4: Discuss the residual vs fitted plot in terms of the assumptions of OLS.

The red line would be flatted to meet the assumption 1 but it violates this assumption. In terms of homoscedasticity,data are clustered in the range of 40 to 50 so it also violets the homoscedasticity condition. In terms of Independence condition, it may have spatial auto correlation in our residuals.

plot(model.1,1)

The chunk below develops a scatterplot filters for log population density that are small (<0) and have high priority re global warming.

Q5: Interpret the scatterplot below. Under predicting their common things in low population density such as Alaska because we are using the population density indicating that we have omitted variable.

low.df<-join.df%>%
  filter(log.pop.dens<0 & priority > 50)%>%
  arrange(log.pop.dens)
low.df


ggplot(data=low.df, aes(x=log.pop.dens, y=priority))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text(aes(label=`Qualifying Name`))+
  xlim(-4, 0.4)+
  xlab("Log(Population Density)")

Q6: Discuss the scatterplot below. We neglect the high population density such as California and New York.

high.df<-join.df%>%
  filter(log.pop.dens>8 & priority > 60)%>%
  arrange(log.pop.dens)
high.df


ggplot(data=high.df, aes(x=log.pop.dens, y=priority))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text(aes(label=`Qualifying Name`))+
  xlab("Log(Population Density)")

Q7: Now it’s your turn. Please do the following:

  1. Change up the explanatory variable to median household income.
join.df<-census.df%>%
  inner_join(climate.df, by=join_by(geoid==geoid))

  1. Develop appropriate hypotheses. Null: The Average Family Income is not correlated whith prioritization of climate change.

  2. Develop a scatterplot and discuss.

ggplot(data=join.df, aes(x=`Average Family Income (In 2022 Inflation Adjusted Dollars)`, y=priority))+

       subtitle = "",
